title: Playwright tackled intruder by instinct: Then reaction set in: 'You don't feel safe anymore'
article: Local playwright Marty Chan spent Sunday trying to recover from a "surreal" home invasion Saturday, when he and his wife were startled awake by a man who later died in police custody.
"To have that sort of violation is a horrible feeling. You don't feel safe anymore. That's what my wife and I are coping with right now," he said Sunday afternoon.
Richard Perry Bellerose, of Edmonton, died shortly after being arrested by police. The investigation into the 30-year-old's death continues. An autopsy is scheduled for this afternoon.
Chan said Bellerose's death was tragic.
He didn't want to speculate on the cause of his death or what sparked the man to break into his home.
Police spokesman Wes Bellmore said police made a "routine" arrest.
"It doesn't sound like (Bellerose) put up a big struggle," he said, adding he doesn't believe pepper spray was used in the arrest.
Bellerose showed signs of physical distress after he was arrested. He was taken to hospital, where he was pronounced dead.
The incident sounds like it was written for the stage.
Chan and his wife, Michelle, a theatre stage director, were sleeping in their cool basement. At about 2:45 a.m., they heard a loud crash upstairs and went to investigate.
The back door of their house, at 106th Avenue and 75th Street, had been kicked in. Furniture was strewn about and a table had been smashed through a window.
Chan said he heard his wife scream in surprise when she saw the intruder. He rushed to the front of the house to see if she was all right.
Michelle stayed inside the house and phoned police while Chan ran outside and tackled the man.
The two wrestled for only a couple of minutes before police arrived, but Chan said it felt like much longer.
"I knew enough that if I let go, I'd be afraid for my safety," he said, adding he did not know the man.
Chan turned the man over to police and saw officers handcuff him, he said. He went back into his house to help his wife, who had cut her wrist on the broken glass of the front screen door.
Chan cut his knees in the scuffle.
Chan chairs the Edmonton Arts Council and has had plays produced across the country.
He currently works in the story department of a children's television show called Mentors, in which two children have a time machine which they use to bring historical figures to the present.
The series is being shot this summer in Edmonton.
Chan said if he could go back in time, he would probably do the same thing in the heat of the moment.
"Now that I'm sitting on the phone, safe, with bandages on my knees, I would say that I wouldn't do that again.
"But at the time, I had just woken up and was reacting to the situation.
"I heard my wife scream and thought she was in trouble. All I knew to do was act."
